stanzas: Kaulana nā pua aʻo Hawaiʻi
Kūpaʻa mahope o ka ʻāina
Hiki mai ka ʻelele o ka loko ʻino
Palapala ʻānunu me ka pākaha
Pane mai Hawaiʻi moku o Keawe
Kōkua nā Hono aʻo Piʻilani
Kākoʻo mai Kauaʻi o Mano
Paʻapū me ke one Kākuhihewa
ʻAʻole aʻe kau i ka pūlima
Maluna o ka pepa o ka ʻenemi
Hoʻohui ʻāina kūʻai hewa
I ka pono sivila aʻo ke kanaka
ʻAʻole mākou aʻe minamina
I ka puʻukālā a ke aupuni
Ua lawa mākou i ka pōhaku
I ka ʻai kamahaʻo o ka ʻāina
Mahope mākou o Liliʻulani
A loaʻa e ka pono o ka ʻāina
Haʻina ʻia mai ana ka puana
Ka poʻe i aloha i ka ʻāina
orig.credit: Ellen Kehoʻohiwaokalani Wright Prendergast (1893); as quoted in Wikipedia's article (Hawaiian Wikipedia)

stanzas: Famous are the children of Hawaiʻi,
steadfast behind the land.
Here comes the messenger of the evil heart,
a greedy document of extortion.
Hawaiʻi, island of Keawe, answers,
the bays of Piʻilani help,
Kauaʻi of Mano supports,
united firmly with the sands of Kākuhihewa.
No one will put the signature
on the paper of the enemy:
annexation, the wrongful sale
of the civil rights of the people.
We do not value
the government's heap of money;
we are content with the stones,
the wondrous food of the land.
We stand behind Liliʻulani
until the rights of the land are won.
Told is the refrain:
the people who love the land.

notes: line 1.1: 'pua', literally 'flowers', is the usual figure for children, descendants.
line 2.1: the island of Hawaiʻi, called after the chief Keawe.
line 2.2: 'nā Hono a Piʻilani', the bays of Piʻilani, i.e. Maui (with Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi and Kahoʻolawe), after the Maui chief Piʻilani.
line 2.3: Kauaʻi of Mano (Manokalanipō), its ancient chief.
line 2.4: the sands of Kākuhihewa, i.e. Oʻahu, after the Oʻahu chief Kākuhihewa.
line 3.3: 'Hoʻohui ʻāina', the joining of lands, annexation; 'kūʻai hewa', a wrongful sale or bargain.
line 4.3: 'pōhaku', stones; the stones are the people's own food, the 'wondrous food of the land', rather than the government's money.
